issues.legal_issue: A landlord satisfies a statutory rent-arrears notice requirement by sending a correctly addressed registered notice through the post, even if it is returned without delivery to the tenant.
material_facts: The landlord sent a registered notice demanding rent arrears to the tenant’s correct address.
The postman called at the address but could not find the tenant or anyone authorised to receive the letter, and it was returned to the sender.
The tenant and the tenant’s servant were away, and no agent had been left to accept letters.
issues.conclusion: Sending the correctly addressed notice by registered post satisfied the statutory notice requirement; actual receipt by the tenant was not necessary.
issues.legal_principle: Under the proviso to section 11(1)(i) and the proviso to section 12(3) of the Jammu and Kashmir Houses and Shops Rent Control Act, 1966, the landlord must send notice through the post. The Court read “served” as sent by post to the tenant’s correct address, and “receipt” as tender of the letter by the postal worker at that address. Once the landlord posts a prepaid registered letter correctly addressed and delivers it to the post office, section 27 of the General Clauses Act supports a presumption of delivery. Requiring actual delivery would make the requirement impractical and unworkable. The Court considered the strict-compliance approach associated with Taylor v. Taylor, but rejected an interpretation that would require the landlord to ensure actual receipt; the cases cited by the tenant concerning returned postal notices did not govern the Court’s interpretation.

predicates.rent_arrears_eviction_proceeding: The landlord brought an eviction proceeding based on the tenant’s failure to pay rent arrears.
predicates.arrears_notice_sent_by_registered_post_t: The landlord sent a registered notice demanding rent arrears to the tenant’s correct address.
predicates.postal_letter_tendered_at_address: A postal worker attempted to deliver the letter at the stated address but could not find the tenant or an authorised recipient.

issues.definition: When an eviction proceeding is based on rent arrears and a correctly addressed registered notice is tendered at the tenant’s address, the notice requirement is satisfied even if the tenant does not receive the letter.

issues.legal_issue: Affixing a notice at the premises is not a required or independently effective method of service when the governing rule specifies postal service alone.
material_facts: After the registered notice was returned, the landlord caused a copy to be affixed to a door of the premises.
The governing rule specified service through the post and did not specify affixture or another alternative method.
issues.conclusion: The affixture had no independent statutory significance and was neither a necessary nor a permissible additional or alternative requirement for service.
issues.legal_principle: The proviso to section 11(1)(i) of the Jammu and Kashmir Houses and Shops Rent Control Act, 1966, prescribes postal service and does not provide for an additional or alternative method. The Court declined to import substituted-service procedures from the Code of Civil Procedure into the statute. Accordingly, if postal dispatch does not satisfy the requirement, affixture cannot cure that failure; if postal dispatch does satisfy it, affixture is unnecessary. The Court did not adopt the strict-performance argument associated with Taylor v. Taylor as a basis for requiring a further method of service.
